title: Brother Lawrence's letters
hook: a little lifting of the heart is enough
tomorrow: what did a mathematician keep sewn inside his coat?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Brother Lawrence's conversations: a cook who kept forgetting God, and kept coming back. Return, and return. Today, the same man, writing letters.

A thumbs-up. A two-letter text. A wave across a parking lot. Small, and nobody thinks they're nothing; a friendship can run on them for weeks. So how little can a prayer be and still count? A whole hour on your knees? Ten minutes with a book? Brother Lawrence got asked versions of that question by friends who wrote to him, and his answer was smaller than they expected.
screen: `A THUMBS-UP. A WAVE.` → `HOW LITTLE CAN A PRAYER BE?` → `SMALLER THAN THEY EXPECTED.`

segments.voice: In his letters, put plainly, Lawrence says you don't have to be in church to be with God. You can make a little chapel of your heart, and step into it now and then, quietly, while you work. How long? He says a little lifting of the heart is enough. A brief remembering of God. One act of inward worship. Even, he writes, for a soldier on the march with a sword in hand: short prayers like that still count, and steady him. So the Christian answer here isn't about length at all. It's about how often you glance up. Now a neighbor who knows this well. The Qur'an says, in Pickthall's translation: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah with much remembrance." Muslims call that remembering dhikr. A physical therapist who says bismillah, in the name of God, under his breath as a patient stands up, is doing a small version of it. Same instinct as Lawrence: God remembered in the middle of the task, briefly, often. And one honest difference. Lawrence's lifting is wordless, a turn of the heart in his own way. Dhikr is often carried by set words from the Qur'an and the Prophet's sayings, in Arabic, the same words across the world. Two neighbors, both glancing up, each in their own words.
screen: `A CHAPEL OF YOUR HEART.` · `EVEN ON THE MARCH, SWORD IN HAND.` · `REMEMBER ALLAH WITH MUCH REMEMBRANCE.` · `WORDLESS, OR SET WORDS.` · then, large: `A LITTLE LIFTING.`

segments.voice: Sit tall and lift your chin a little, the way you look up when someone you love walks into the room. Hold that small lift for one breath, then let it settle. Do it a few more times in the sit: lift, settle, lift.
Brother Lawrence's letters. Advice to friends from a kitchen: a chapel in the heart, and a prayer as small as a glance.
Carry this: a little lifting, which Lawrence says is enough even with a sword in your hand. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Christians follow Brother Lawrence's advice with brief turns to God through the day, sometimes on the hour; Muslims practice dhikr, the remembrance of God, often in short phrases from the Qur'an and the Prophet's sayings.

chat.says: Pop's PT whispers 'bismillah' each time Pop stands. is that like Brother Lawrence's little lifting?
options: In one way: both turn to God for a second mid-task. His has set words; Lawrence's was wordless.
Yes, it's exactly the same thing, just in Arabic. Every religion has the same prayer.
Not really. A real prayer needs time set aside; a whisper at work doesn't count.
chat.meaning: Shared: remembering God briefly, often, mid-task (Lawrence; Qur'an 33:41). Different: dhikr is often carried by set Arabic words; Lawrence's lift was wordless.

Brother Lawrence.meaning: a French Carmelite lay brother who worked in the kitchen

Pickthall.meaning: Marmaduke Pickthall, a Muslim who translated the Qur'an into English

dhikr.meaning: Arabic: remembrance; Muslim practice of remembering God

bismillah.meaning: Arabic: in the name of God
